comprehensive.title: Comprehensive Bank
comprehensive.description: Full reference with every testable detail

questions.question: Why is cloud computing described as a disruptive technology?

options.label: A
options.text: Adding more components, such as another server or storage array

options.label: B
options.text: Access services from different devices and locations over a network

options.label: C
options.text: It can significantly transform businesses, economies, and lives

options.label: D
options.text: Manual provisioning can be slow, cumbersome, and error-prone

questions.rationale: Cloud adoption can transform business models and is expected to have broad economic and social effects.

questions.question: Which trend is identified as influencing cloud adoption?
questions.rationale: Mobility, Big Data, and social media are cited as technology trends driving cloud adoption.

questions.question: According to the module, cloud adoption is increasingly becoming what type of decision?

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced time to provision IT resources

questions.rationale: Organizations increasingly view cloud adoption as strategic to business and operations.

questions.question: Which organization is identified as the source of the cloud-computing definition used in the module?
questions.rationale: The module uses the NIST SP 800-145 definition.

questions.question: Which option best defines a cloud in this module?

options.label: A
options.text: Through economy of scale and resource sharing

options.label: B
options.text: A collection of network-accessible IT resources

options.label: C
options.text: By maintaining additional recoverable copies of data

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing resources to meet greater demand

questions.rationale: A cloud is a collection of network-accessible hardware and software resources.

questions.question: Where are the hardware and software resources of a cloud typically deployed?
questions.rationale: Cloud infrastructure resources are deployed in data centers.

questions.question: What does the cloud model enable consumers to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Adding resources to a single component

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing resources to meet greater demand

options.label: D
options.text: Hire a provider's IT resources as services

questions.rationale: Consumers hire required IT assets as services from a provider's infrastructure.

questions.question: Which of the following may be offered as a cloud service?

options.label: A
options.text: Employees may use non-company devices for business work

options.label: B
options.text: No; applications typically invoke them through procedure calls

options.label: C
options.text: Storage, processing capacity, and software-development tools

options.label: D
options.text: Processor time, network bandwidth, and storage capacity

questions.rationale: Cloud services may combine storage, processing, applications, and development/deployment tools.

questions.question: What happens to a cloud resource after a consumer releases it?

options.label: B
options.text: It is returned to the shared pool

options.label: D
options.text: Adding resources to a single component

questions.rationale: Released resources return to the pool and can be reallocated.

questions.question: Which interaction model generally describes communication between cloud consumers and compute systems?
questions.rationale: Consumers act as clients that send requests to compute systems acting as servers.

questions.question: Which item is part of a data center's supporting infrastructure?

options.label: A
options.text: Access services from different devices and locations over a network

options.label: B
options.text: Manual provisioning can be slow, cumbersome, and error-prone

options.label: C
options.text: HVAC systems, backup generators, and fire-suppression equipment

options.label: D
options.text: Adding more components, such as another server or storage array

questions.rationale: Data centers include power, cooling, safety, and physical-support systems.

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.text: It provides visibility into consumption and service-level verification

options.label: D
options.text: Virtually unlimited and obtainable in any quantity at any time

questions.question: How is cloud computing similar to an electricity utility?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service

options.label: D
options.text: Consumers use a service without owning its production infrastructure and pay according to use or subscription

questions.question: Why can cloud computing help smaller companies compete?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: It provides access to required IT resources without cost-prohibitive ownership

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers hire required resources using pay-per-use or subscription pricing

options.label: D
options.text: The ability to rapidly provision and release resources according to demand

questions.rationale: Smaller organizations can obtain resources that would otherwise require expensive ownership.

questions.question: Which list contains all five essential cloud characteristics specified by NIST?

options.label: A
options.text: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service

options.label: B
options.text: The provider handles infrastructure updates, renewals, and much of the underlying management

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers may choose a broad region without knowing the exact resource location

options.label: D
options.text: It provides access to required IT resources without cost-prohibitive ownership

questions.rationale: These are the five essential characteristics used throughout the module.

options.text: Employees may use non-company devices for business work

questions.question: At which layer do applications interact to exchange data over a network?

questions.question: Which protocol is typically used by applications to transmit data over the web?

questions.question: Which two approaches are identified as primary bases for web services?

options.label: A

options.text: The provider handles infrastructure updates, renewals, and much of the underlying management

options.label: B
options.text: It provides access to required IT resources without cost-prohibitive ownership

questions.question: Cloud computing adoption is increasingly treated as a strategic business decision.
questions.rationale: Organizations increasingly see cloud as essential to strategy and operations.

questions.question: Mobility, Big Data, and social media can influence cloud adoption.
questions.rationale: All three trends are explicitly mentioned.

questions.question: A cloud consists only of software resources and never includes hardware.
questions.rationale: A cloud includes shared pools of both hardware and software resources.

questions.question: Cloud resources are accessed over a network such as the Internet or an intranet.
questions.rationale: Network accessibility is fundamental to the module's definition.

questions.question: Consumers must always interact with provider staff before provisioning a cloud resource.
questions.rationale: On-demand self-service allows automatic provisioning without provider human interaction.

questions.question: Released cloud resources can return to a shared pool for reallocation.
questions.rationale: Pool members are dynamically assigned, released, and reassigned.

questions.question: A data center includes only servers and has no supporting power or cooling infrastructure.
questions.rationale: Data centers also include UPS, generators, HVAC, fire suppression, secure access, and other support systems.

questions.question: A cloud infrastructure may span multiple geographically distributed data centers.
questions.rationale: Connected data centers may collectively form the infrastructure.

questions.question: Cloud consumers must understand exactly how provider infrastructure generates and distributes every service.
questions.rationale: The infrastructure is abstracted from consumers, similar to a utility.

questions.question: Cloud pricing may be based on a subscription or on resource consumption.
questions.rationale: Both pricing approaches are described.

questions.question: On-demand self-service is one of NIST's five essential cloud characteristics.
questions.rationale: It is one of the five listed characteristics.

questions.question: In this module, a cloud can itself be a consumer of another cloud.
questions.rationale: The terminology note explicitly allows this.

questions.question: A self-service portal is normally a web-based interface through which consumers view and request services.
questions.rationale: The portal exposes the provider's catalog and request process.

questions.question: A service catalog contains no pricing or service-function information.
questions.rationale: It may include offerings, prices, functions, and request processes.

questions.question: On-demand self-service tends to increase resource-provisioning time.
questions.rationale: It reduces provisioning time by removing slow acquisition and manual configuration steps.

questions.question: Broad network access requires every consumer device to use identical hardware and software.
questions.rationale: Standard mechanisms support heterogeneous client platforms.

questions.question: Cloud access may be provided through desktops, laptops, tablets, phones, and thin clients.
questions.rationale: These heterogeneous endpoints are listed in the notes.

questions.question: The Application Layer is the top layer in the OSI and TCP/IP discussions presented in the notes.
questions.rationale: Applications interact at the top-most Application Layer.

questions.question: HTTP is described as an Application Layer protocol commonly used for data transmission.
questions.rationale: Applications commonly use HTTP to exchange data.

questions.question: Web services force all communicating applications to be written in the same programming language.
questions.rationale: They enable interoperability among applications developed in different languages.

questions.question: XML may be used to format web-service data that is transmitted using HTTP.
questions.rationale: This is the mechanism described in the notes.

questions.question: Web services always require a user interface.
questions.rationale: They are invoked by applications and need not expose a user interface.

questions.question: SOAP and REST are not the two main web-service approaches identified in the module.
questions.rationale: Correct: SOAP and REST are the two main web-service approaches identified in the module.

questions.question: Resource pooling permanently assigns every resource to one consumer.
questions.rationale: Resources can be dynamically assigned, released, and reassigned among consumers.

questions.question: Consumers generally know and control the exact physical location of every pooled resource.
questions.rationale: Exact location is generally abstracted, though a high-level region may be selectable.

questions.question: Resource pooling can improve provider utilization and flexibility.
questions.rationale: Pooling allows resources to be allocated according to demand.

questions.question: Multi-tenancy means that multiple independent consumers share a common set of underlying resources.
questions.rationale: Multiple tenants are served while remaining logically isolated.

questions.question: Sharing physical resources means that tenants' activities and data cannot be isolated.
questions.rationale: Effective logical isolation is maintained despite resource sharing.

questions.question: Virtualization is useful for cloud resource pooling, but it is not an absolute requirement for every cloud.
questions.rationale: The notes explicitly distinguish enablement from strict necessity.

questions.question: Rapid elasticity allows resources to scale outward and inward according to demand.
questions.rationale: Resources may be rapidly provisioned and released.

questions.question: Rapid elasticity requires consumers to retain idle peak capacity permanently.
questions.rationale: Resources can be released after peak demand, reducing over-provisioning.

questions.question: Elastic provisioning is commonly automated because manual work can be slow and error-prone.
questions.rationale: Automation supports dynamic response to monitored usage.

questions.question: Scalability is described as always unplanned and instantaneous.
questions.rationale: Scalability is generally planned according to estimated growth and capacity needs.

questions.question: Adding memory to one compute system is an example of vertical scaling.
questions.rationale: Vertical scaling adds resources to a single component.

questions.question: Adding another compute system is an example of horizontal scaling.
questions.rationale: Horizontal scaling adds more components to the infrastructure.

questions.question: Measured service supports billing based on resource usage.
questions.rationale: Metering tracks consumer usage for billing.

questions.question: Resource monitoring has no role in capacity or service planning.
questions.rationale: Monitoring reveals demand and helps determine when resources should be added or released.

questions.question: Metering can improve transparency for both provider and consumer.
questions.rationale: Usage reports support billing transparency and service-level verification.

questions.question: Cloud business agility can shorten time-to-market and support experimentation.
questions.rationale: Rapid provisioning supports faster deployment and innovation.

questions.question: Cloud computing always increases consumers' up-front capital expenditure.

questions.question: Program execution, data storage, communication, backup, and security-policy enforcement may occur at the physical layer.

questions.question: The virtual layer makes physical resources appear as virtual resources.
questions.rationale: This is its abstraction function.

questions.question: Virtualization prevents multi-tenancy and reduces physical-resource utilization.
questions.rationale: It enables multi-tenancy and improves utilization.

questions.question: Virtualization software can create pools from which virtual resources are provisioned.
questions.rationale: Pooling is one of its responsibilities.

questions.question: A virtual machine, LUN, and virtual network are examples of virtual resources.
questions.rationale: All three are cited.

questions.rationale: The virtual layer may be omitted or only part of the infrastructure may be virtualized.

questions.question: The control layer cannot operate over either the virtual layer or directly over the physical layer.
questions.rationale: Correct: The control layer can operate over either the virtual layer or directly over the physical layer.

questions.question: Control software initiates resource-configuration, pooling, and provisioning requests.
questions.rationale: These are control-layer functions.

questions.question: If no virtual layer exists, control-layer requests cannot be fulfilled.
questions.rationale: They can pass directly to the physical layer.

questions.question: The control layer hides all resources from the service layer.
questions.rationale: It exposes physical and/or virtual resources to support the service layer.

questions.question: A workflow is a series of interrelated tasks that performs a business operation.
questions.rationale: This is the notes definition.

questions.question: Orchestration requires dependent tasks to be executed manually one at a time.
questions.rationale: It groups and sequences them in an automated workflow.

questions.question: Orchestration may invoke tasks in control, BC, security, and service-management entities.
questions.rationale: It coordinates provisioning across them.

questions.question: Cloud consumers interact with services through the service layer.

questions.rationale: It may include descriptions, types, costs, SLAs, and security mechanisms.

questions.rationale: They are invoked after service failure.

questions.rationale: It supports all five layers.

questions.rationale: These tools are listed technical controls.

questions.rationale: It starts from the physical layer.

questions.question: Brownfield deployment discards every existing infrastructure entity and starts from nothing.

questions.rationale: Additional packages can be combined for capacity and performance.

questions.rationale: It reduces integration work before cloud-service deployment.

questions.rationale: Single management software is listed.

questions.rationale: Additional security mechanisms should still be deployed.

questions.question: CSA and ENISA are cited as sources for the cloud-threat list.
questions.rationale: Both organizations are named.

questions.question: The lesson lists data leakage, data loss, account hijacking, and insecure APIs as threats.
questions.rationale: All are included.

questions.question: Data leakage requires authorized access to public information.
questions.rationale: It is unauthorized access to confidential consumer data.

questions.question: A compromised password database may enable impersonation.
questions.rationale: Stolen credentials expose consumer accounts and data.

questions.question: Poor traffic segregation and weak encryption cannot contribute to leakage.
questions.rationale: Correct: Poor traffic segregation and weak encryption can contribute to leakage.

questions.question: MFA can reduce breach likelihood after password compromise.
questions.rationale: The password is only part of the credential set.

questions.question: A cross-VM side-channel attack includes placement and information extraction.
questions.rationale: These are its two stages.

questions.question: VM placement attempts to keep the malicious VM away from the target.
questions.rationale: The attacker seeks co-location with the target VM.

questions.question: Keystrokes, cache data, and network traffic may reveal target-VM information.
questions.rationale: All are extraction signals.

questions.question: Data shredding cannot remove residual data after service discontinuation.
questions.rationale: Correct: Data shredding can remove residual data after service discontinuation.

questions.question: Data loss can result from accidental deletion or natural disaster.
questions.rationale: Both causes are listed.

questions.question: Providers should omit data-loss penalties from service contracts.
questions.rationale: Terms, conditions, and penalties should be included.

questions.question: Backup and replication are not BC/DR options for data loss.
questions.rationale: Correct: Backup and replication are BC/DR options for data loss.

questions.question: Phishing is a social-engineering attack.
questions.rationale: It deceives users into revealing credentials.

questions.question: A phishing site openly identifies itself as malicious.
questions.rationale: It masquerades as a legitimate site.

questions.question: Keystroke-logging malware cannot capture and send credentials to an attacker.
questions.rationale: Correct: Keystroke-logging malware can capture and send credentials to an attacker.

questions.question: A hijacker may manipulate data, falsify information, or redirect clients.
questions.rationale: These post-takeover actions are listed.

questions.question: A man-in-the-middle attack eavesdrops on a network channel.
questions.rationale: It captures transmitted credentials.

questions.question: MFA, IPSec, IDPS, and firewalls are listed account-hijacking controls.
questions.rationale: All four are named.

questions.question: Cloud APIs are not used for provisioning, configuration, monitoring, management, and orchestration.
questions.rationale: Correct: Cloud APIs are used for provisioning, configuration, monitoring, management, and orchestration.

questions.question: The security of cloud services is independent of API security.
questions.rationale: Service security depends on secure APIs.

questions.question: APIs should require authentication and authorization and avoid buffer overflows.
questions.rationale: These are secure-development practices.

questions.question: API access should not be restricted to authorized users.
questions.rationale: Correct: API access should be restricted to authorized users.

questions.question: DoS seeks to prevent legitimate resource or service access.
questions.rationale: This is its objective.

questions.question: DoS can target compute, network, or storage resources.
questions.rationale: All are listed targets.

questions.question: Bandwidth flooding and CPU consumption are not DoS examples.
questions.rationale: Correct: Bandwidth flooding and CPU consumption are DoS examples.

questions.question: Resetting TCP sessions and corrupting DNS cache may cause DoS.
questions.rationale: Both exploit protocol services.

questions.question: Cloud DoS can produce non-productive charges for the victim.
questions.rationale: Attack resource use may be billed.

questions.question: DDoS uses several systems in a coordinated attack.
questions.rationale: Multiple agents attack simultaneously.

questions.question: DDoS agents initiate the attack before receiving a master command.
questions.rationale: They begin after the command arrives.

questions.question: Resource-consumption limits cannot reduce DoS and DDoS impact.
questions.rationale: Correct: Resource-consumption limits can reduce DoS and DDoS impact.

questions.question: Traffic from an over-limit IP address may be blocked.
questions.rationale: This is a first line of defense.

questions.question: Per-system resource limits add another line of defense.
questions.rationale: Host quotas supplement traffic blocking.

questions.question: Perimeter tools fully eliminate malicious-insider risk.
questions.rationale: Authorized insiders may bypass outsider defenses.

questions.question: A malicious insider may be a current or former employee, contractor, or partner.
questions.rationale: CERT's definition includes these roles.

questions.question: Malicious insiders intentionally misuse authorized access.
questions.rationale: Intentional misuse can harm CIA.

questions.question: Former employees may know exploitable infrastructure weaknesses.
questions.rationale: Their knowledge creates risk.

questions.question: Employee accounts should be disabled immediately after separation.
questions.rationale: Prompt disabling is a listed control.

questions.question: Security auditing, encryption, and segregation of duties reduce insider risk.
questions.rationale: All are listed controls.

questions.question: Cloud computing resources cannot accelerate encryption-key cracking.
questions.rationale: Large cloud capacity may reduce years to minutes or hours.

questions.question: Distributing pirated software is not an example of cloud-service abuse.
questions.rationale: Correct: Distributing pirated software is an example of cloud-service abuse.

questions.question: Technical tools alone are sufficient to eliminate service abuse.
questions.rationale: Acceptable-use agreements are also needed.

questions.question: Due diligence includes understanding incident response, encryption, governance, compliance, and monitoring responsibilities.
questions.rationale: All are listed responsibilities.

questions.question: Hybrid-cloud and broker scenarios reduce the need to evaluate external providers.
questions.rationale: Cross-provider dependencies increase due-diligence needs.

questions.question: A broker should assess provider services, terms, and security controls.
questions.rationale: Evaluation reduces consumer risk.

questions.question: Consumer risk profiles help determine acceptable risk levels.
questions.rationale: Risk must align with consumer tolerance.

questions.question: Failure of memory or storage separation cannot expose one tenant's data to another.
questions.rationale: Correct: Failure of memory or storage separation can expose one tenant's data to another.

questions.question: Hyperjacking installs a rogue hypervisor that controls a compute system.
questions.rationale: This is the definition.

questions.question: A rogue hypervisor may run unauthorized VMs for further attacks.
questions.rationale: This capability is described.

questions.question: Hyperjacking is easy to detect without low-level inspection.
questions.rationale: Detection is difficult and may inspect memory and registers.

questions.question: Securing TCB components may help prevent hyperjacking.
questions.rationale: The hypervisor belongs to the trusted base.

questions.question: Loss of compliance can involve failure to demonstrate adherence.
questions.rationale: Evidence as well as adherence is required.

questions.question: Vulnerability assessment scans compute, storage, and network resources.
questions.rationale: Scanning seeks potential vulnerabilities.

questions.question: PCI compliance governs handling of credit-card data.
questions.rationale: PCI is the example.

questions.question: Cloud-provider contracts may prohibit consumer vulnerability scans.
questions.rationale: Scans may disrupt other tenants.

questions.question: If scanning is not prohibited, brokers and consumers may rely on provider assessment results.
questions.rationale: Correct: If scanning is prohibited, brokers and consumers may rely on provider assessment results.

questions.question: Outsourcing always strengthens provider governance control.
questions.rationale: It may diminish governance effectiveness.

questions.question: Third-party control changes can affect provider terms and commitments.
questions.rationale: Outsourced controls influence provider obligations.

questions.question: Missing third-party compliance evidence cannot put the provider at risk.
questions.rationale: Correct: Missing third-party compliance evidence can put the provider at risk.

questions.question: Providers deploy security mechanisms to prepare for the listed threats.
questions.rationale: The following lessons cover those mechanisms.
